LONDON, England (CNN) -- As familiar and reassuring as the map of the world is, there is only so much that physical geography can tell us about the state of the planet. Forest loss: This cartogram shows areas where the worst deforestation occured from 1990 to 2000. A new book, The Atlas of the Real World, has redrawn the map giving vivid new insights and bringing economic, social and environmental data to life. Not since the German meteorologist, Alfred Wegener, sketched out the first detailed theories of continental drift has the world appeared so misshapen, so otherworldly. The 366 cartograms (statistical maps) which make up the book twist, shrink and distend countries and continents into all sorts of shapes and sizes. The book and the accompanying Web site were devised by Daniel Dorling, professor of human geography at the UK's University of Sheffield, Anna Barford, a research associate at Sheffield and Mark Newman, a professor of physics at the University of Michigan. Work on the project began in earnest in 2006 when Dorling teamed up with Newman, who had co-created a new software technique for creating equal area cartograms the year before. With the software in place, the painstaking task of assembling the data began. The information was drawn from a variety of organizations including the United Nations, the World Health Organization and the World Bank. For ease of visual comparison, territories are split into 12 geographical regions -- e.g. blue for North America, brown for Northern Africa -- and shading marks out specific countries. The range of subjects is impressive, from greenhouse gas emissions, wealth and disease to more obscure data about numbers of dentists and working tractors. John Pritchard, research assistant at University of Sheffield and part of the team working on the project, told CNN: "I think the maps of disease are particularly shocking and bring home the scale of the problem in Africa better than a table of statistics does." Indeed, the map of malaria deaths is striking: 94 percent of deaths from malaria occur in Africa, making the continent appear like a vast bloated blob. The rest of the world is reduced to a disparate series of veiny streaks. There are other sobering statistics to consider. In June 2008, Principal Voices spoke to Head of Research at Oxfam GB Duncan Green about strategies to eradicate poverty. Green talked about the education being crucial to breaking the cycle of poverty, particularly for girls. The new atlas's Girls not at Primary School cartogram graphically illustrates the lack of female education in many parts of the developing world. Team members are currently working on a map of languages and soon hope to be producing animated maps. "We have a series of maps that show deaths at various stages, which would be particularly suited to an animation, and we now have a PhD student looking at extending the Web site, including ways of mapping flow." Pritchard said.

LONDON, England (CNN) — Although the standard world map may feel familiar and dependable, physical geography alone can reveal only a limited picture of the planet’s condition.

One cartogram on forest loss highlights the places that experienced the most severe deforestation between 1990 and 2000. A new publication, *The Atlas of the Real World*, reshapes the world map to offer fresh, striking perspectives and to make economic, social and environmental information visually vivid.

Not since German meteorologist Alfred Wegener first set out detailed ideas about continental drift has the Earth looked so distorted and unfamiliar. The book contains 366 cartograms, or statistical maps, that stretch, compress and warp nations and continents into many different forms and proportions.

The atlas, along with its related Web site, was created by Daniel Dorling, professor of human geography at the University of Sheffield in the UK; Anna Barford, a research associate at Sheffield; and Mark Newman, professor of physics at the University of Michigan.

The project began in earnest in 2006, when Dorling joined forces with Newman, who the previous year had helped develop a new software method for producing equal-area cartograms. Once that software was available, the team began the detailed and labor-intensive process of gathering data.

Their information came from numerous bodies, among them the United Nations, the World Health Organization and the World Bank. To make visual comparisons easier, the maps divide territories into 12 geographic regions — for example, North America is shown in blue and Northern Africa in brown — while shading is used to distinguish individual countries.

The subjects covered are wide-ranging, including greenhouse gas emissions, wealth and disease, as well as less commonly mapped figures such as the number of dentists and working tractors.

John Pritchard, a research assistant at the University of Sheffield and a member of the project team, told CNN: “I think the maps of disease are particularly shocking and bring home the scale of the problem in Africa better than a table of statistics does.”

The malaria mortality map is especially powerful. Since 94 percent of malaria deaths take place in Africa, the continent is depicted as an enormous swollen mass, while the rest of the world appears as a scattered collection of thin, vein-like strips.

Other statistics are equally serious. In June 2008, Principal Voices interviewed Duncan Green, Head of Research at Oxfam GB, about approaches to eliminating poverty. Green emphasized that education is essential for breaking the cycle of poverty, especially for girls.

The atlas’s cartogram titled “Girls not at Primary School” makes the shortage of female education across many areas of the developing world immediately visible.

Members of the team are now developing a map of languages and hope soon to create animated maps. Pritchard said: “We have a series of maps that show deaths at various stages, which would be particularly suited to an animation, and we now have a PhD student looking at extending the Web site, including ways of mapping flow.”

# New Atlas Shows the World as Data — Not Geography

**By Staff Writer**

A new way of looking at the world is challenging one of the most familiar images on Earth: the map.

*The Atlas of the Real World* uses cartograms — maps that resize countries and regions according to data rather than land area — to show global inequality, consumption, health, population and environmental impact in ways traditional maps often cannot.

On a conventional map, Canada and Russia dominate the page because of their vast territories. In a cartogram, however, size depends on the subject being measured. A country with a large population, a high gross domestic product or heavy carbon emissions may swell dramatically, while a geographically large but less populous or less economically powerful country may shrink.

The result is a world that looks distorted at first glance — but is designed to reveal patterns that standard geography can hide.

## A world reshaped by numbers

In *The Atlas of the Real World*, countries are redrawn according to hundreds of indicators, including wealth, education, disease, migration, resource use and pollution.

A population cartogram makes India and China appear enormous, reflecting their billions of residents. A map based on global income expands North America, Western Europe and parts of East Asia, while many poorer regions become smaller. A map showing carbon dioxide emissions enlarges the world’s major industrial economies, highlighting the uneven responsibility for climate change.

The visual impact is immediate: the “real world” changes depending on what is being measured.

Cartograms work by preserving the general location of countries while altering their size to match statistical values. The technique allows readers to compare global data spatially, turning abstract numbers into a visual story.

## Seeing inequality differently

The book’s central message is that political maps can give a misleading sense of balance. Every country has a place on the map, but not every country has the same influence, population, wealth or environmental footprint.

When mapped by military spending, economic production or access to health care, the world looks dramatically different from the familiar classroom map. Some nations balloon far beyond their geographic borders; others nearly disappear.

That distortion is the point.

By changing the size of countries, the atlas forces readers to confront disparities that can be difficult to grasp in tables or charts. It makes visible the concentration of wealth, the scale of poverty, the uneven spread of disease and the global consequences of consumption.

## Environment and responsibility

Environmental cartograms are among the book’s most striking images. Maps based on energy use, emissions, deforestation or ecological impact show how the pressures placed on the planet are far from evenly distributed.

Countries with high levels of consumption expand, while nations that contribute less to global environmental damage shrink. In the context of climate change, these maps raise questions about responsibility, development and fairness.

They also show the gap between where environmental harm is produced and where its effects may be felt most severely.

## More than a map book

*The Atlas of the Real World* is not simply a collection of unusual maps. It is an argument about how data can change perception.

Traditional maps tell us where countries are. Cartograms ask a different question: how much do they matter in relation to a particular issue?

For readers used to seeing the world divided by borders and landmass, the atlas offers a different kind of geography — one shaped by people, money, health, power and pollution.

Its maps may look strange, but that strangeness is what makes them effective. They show that the world we think we know can look very different when measured by the realities that define everyday life.

# New statistical world maps expose stark global inequalities

Newly compiled statistical world maps are offering a striking visual account of global inequality, showing how where a person is born can still shape their chances of living a long life, accessing health care, earning a stable income or benefiting from basic public services.

Using data from the United Nations, the World Health Organization and the World Bank, the maps compare countries across a range of indicators, including life expectancy, infant and maternal mortality, income levels, access to clean water, education, health spending and population growth. Together, they present a detailed picture of a world where progress is real but unevenly shared.

The visualizations show familiar divides between high-income and low-income nations, but they also highlight regional contrasts that are often hidden in global averages. Wealthier countries in North America, Western Europe and parts of East Asia tend to show higher life expectancy, broader access to health services and stronger economic output. Many countries in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia continue to face heavier burdens of disease, lower incomes and weaker infrastructure.

Public health indicators reveal some of the sharpest gaps. WHO data shows that life expectancy remains significantly higher in richer nations, where health systems are better funded and preventive care is more widely available. In contrast, countries with limited health budgets often face higher rates of preventable deaths, including deaths linked to childbirth, infectious disease and lack of access to basic treatment.

The maps also underline how economic inequality and health inequality are closely connected. World Bank data on gross domestic product per capita shows that countries with higher national income are generally better positioned to invest in hospitals, sanitation, education and social protection. But the relationship is not automatic. Some middle-income countries outperform wealthier peers on certain health or education measures, suggesting that policy choices can make a major difference.

UN population data adds another layer to the picture. Many of the world’s fastest-growing populations are in countries already facing pressure on schools, housing, employment and health systems. Meanwhile, many richer countries are aging rapidly, raising questions about labor shortages, pension systems and the long-term cost of care for older adults.

Access to clean water and sanitation remains one of the clearest markers of inequality. While these services are nearly universal in most high-income countries, millions of people elsewhere still lack reliable access. The consequences are far-reaching, affecting child health, school attendance, food security and economic opportunity.

Education data tells a similar story. Countries with higher literacy rates and longer average years of schooling often show stronger economic resilience and better health outcomes. In regions where children—especially girls—face barriers to education, the effects can extend across generations, limiting earnings, increasing health risks and reducing political participation.

Experts say the power of these maps lies in their ability to make complex data immediately visible. A table of statistics can show differences between countries, but a map can reveal patterns across entire regions—coastlines where development clusters, landlocked areas facing infrastructure challenges, or neighboring countries with sharply different outcomes.

Still, researchers caution that maps can simplify reality. National averages may conceal deep inequalities within countries, including disparities by race, gender, ethnicity, income, rural location or migration status. A country shaded as relatively prosperous may still have communities living without adequate housing, health care or clean water.

The maps also reflect the limits of available data. In some countries, especially those affected by conflict or political instability, statistics may be incomplete, outdated or difficult to verify. International agencies such as the UN, WHO and World Bank rely on government reporting, surveys and modeling, which can vary in quality.

Even with those caveats, the overall message is clear: global development has advanced, but the benefits remain uneven. Child mortality has fallen dramatically over recent decades, more children are in school, and extreme poverty has declined from historic levels. Yet the maps show that geography, income and governance still play a powerful role in determining life outcomes.

For policymakers, the visual evidence may help identify where investment is most urgently needed. Health funding, education access, climate resilience, clean water infrastructure and poverty reduction remain central to closing the gaps.

For the public, the maps offer something more immediate: a way to see inequality not as an abstract concept, but as a global pattern that affects billions of lives.

They show a world connected by trade, migration, climate and technology—but still divided by opportunity.

# The World, Redrawn: How *The Atlas of the Real World* Changes What Maps Can Tell Us

Open a conventional world atlas and the planet appears reassuringly familiar: Africa broad and central, Greenland immense, Europe comfortably detailed, the Pacific stretching wide between continents. But this familiar image is also a habit of mind. It shows land area, not human experience. It tells us where territory lies, but not where people live, where wealth accumulates, where children are born, where carbon is emitted, where disease strikes, or where political power is concentrated.

*The Atlas of the Real World: Mapping the Way We Live*, together with its accompanying website, set out to challenge that habit. Instead of asking readers to see the world as a fixed arrangement of landmasses, the project asks a more unsettling question: What would the world look like if countries were sized according to the realities that shape human life?

The answer is a collection of vivid, distorted, and often startling maps known as equal-area cartograms. In these maps, every country is resized according to a particular statistic. A country with a large share of the world’s population swells; one with a small share shrinks. A nation that produces a large amount of carbon dioxide expands; a country with little industrial output may nearly disappear. The result is not a map for navigation, but a map for understanding.

## A Different Kind of Accuracy

At first glance, the cartograms can look strange, even playful. Continents bulge and contract. Borders bend. Familiar shapes become elastic. Yet the distortion is the point. Traditional maps are accurate in one sense: they preserve geography, or at least attempt to represent the Earth’s surface on a flat page. But they can be misleading in another sense, because physical size is often a poor guide to social, economic, or environmental importance.

Equal-area cartograms reverse that logic. They preserve proportionality not by land, but by data. If a map shows population, then each person is given roughly equal visual weight. If it shows wealth, then each dollar of gross domestic product is represented by comparable space. The “area” on the page becomes an argument: this is where the phenomenon is concentrated.

That approach gives *The Atlas of the Real World* its force. It turns statistics into geography and geography into a story about inequality, globalization, consumption, health, migration, and power.

A conventional map may make Canada and Russia loom large because of their vast territories. A population cartogram shrinks them dramatically and enlarges India, China, Japan, Indonesia, Nigeria, and parts of Europe. A wealth cartogram inflates North America, Western Europe, and Japan. A map of HIV prevalence, child mortality, military spending, toy exports, or international tourism reshapes the globe in different ways, each one revealing a pattern that a table of numbers might conceal.

## The Team Behind the Atlas

The atlas grew out of work by researchers interested in the relationship between geography, social inequality, and public communication. Among the key figures associated with the project are geographer Danny Dorling, known for his work on social and spatial inequality; physicist and network scientist Mark Newman, whose cartogram algorithms helped make the maps possible; and researcher Anna Barford, whose work has focused on development, poverty, and global social change.

Their collaboration brought together technical expertise, geographic imagination, and a commitment to making complex global data accessible to a broad audience. The result was not simply an academic exercise but a public-facing project: an atlas and a website that invited readers to explore the world through hundreds of thematic maps.

The accompanying website, widely associated with the Worldmapper project, expanded the reach of the atlas beyond the printed page. Online, users could browse cartograms by theme, compare countries, and encounter global data visually rather than as a dense statistical archive. For teachers, journalists, students, policy specialists, and curious readers, the site became a way to ask sharper questions about the world.

The project’s genius lies in its clarity. It does not require advanced training to grasp the meaning of a swollen region or a shrunken one. The maps are immediate. They compress enormous datasets into images that can be absorbed quickly, debated easily, and remembered long after the numbers have faded.

## Seeing Inequality at Planetary Scale

Many of the atlas’s most powerful maps concern inequality. A map of income or wealth shows a world in which economic power is distributed very differently from population. Regions that contain large numbers of people do not always command comparable shares of global resources. North America and Western Europe balloon; many poorer countries contract.

Other maps complicate that picture. A cartogram of children, for example, enlarges parts of Africa and South Asia, emphasizing where the world’s youngest populations live. A map of elderly people reshapes the world again, highlighting aging societies in Europe, Japan, and elsewhere. Population is not one story but many: youth, age, birth, mortality, migration, urbanization.

Health maps can be especially sobering. When countries are resized by cases of particular diseases or by deaths from preventable causes, familiar geopolitical assumptions fall away. The reader is confronted not with abstract suffering but with a spatial pattern of vulnerability. The maps show how poverty, public health infrastructure, conflict, climate, and history combine to shape life chances.

Environmental maps introduce another kind of moral geography. Carbon emissions, ecological footprints, energy use, and resource consumption often enlarge countries that are already wealthy. These images make visible the uneven responsibility for environmental change. They also reveal the tension between population size and consumption: a country may contain many people but produce relatively little pollution per person, while a smaller wealthy country may occupy a huge space on an emissions cartogram.

This is where the atlas becomes more than a visualization project. It becomes a tool for ethical reflection. Who uses the world’s resources? Who bears the consequences? Who benefits from global trade? Who is left exposed?

## The Shock of the Familiar Made Strange

Part of the appeal of *The Atlas of the Real World* is that it makes the familiar strange. Readers know the outline of the world so well that deviations from it feel dramatic. When the United States expands on a map of military spending or shrinks on a map of certain forms of manufacturing employment, the distortion carries meaning. When Africa grows on maps of children or disease burden but contracts on maps of wealth, the contrast is impossible to ignore.

Cartograms are particularly effective because they work through comparison. No single map tells the whole story. Instead, the atlas encourages readers to move from one map to another, watching the world transform. Population, income, exports, imports, education, mortality, greenhouse gases, internet use, migration—each theme produces a different planet.

This repeated redrawing teaches an important lesson: there is no single “real” map of the world. Every map selects, emphasizes, simplifies, and omits. The familiar political map is no exception. It privileges territory and state borders. The atlas’s cartograms privilege lived conditions and measurable phenomena. In doing so, they remind readers that maps are not neutral windows onto reality. They are arguments about what matters.

## A Website for Exploration

The accompanying website extends that argument interactively and educationally. By making the maps available online, the project allows users to wander through global patterns in a way that a traditional atlas cannot fully support. Maps can be grouped by theme—population, health, wealth, education, environment, trade, communication, transport—and compared quickly.

The digital format also helps democratize access. A printed atlas can sit on a library shelf or coffee table; a website can circulate in classrooms, lectures, newsrooms, and social media. Its maps are designed to provoke curiosity. Why does this region expand here but disappear there? Why does a wealthy country dominate one measure but not another? What historical forces explain this pattern?

In this sense, the website functions not only as a companion to the book but as a public data platform. It invites users to treat maps as questions rather than answers.

## The Power and Limits of Cartograms

Like all forms of visualization, equal-area cartograms have limits. They simplify complex data. They depend on the quality and comparability of international statistics. They can make small countries hard to recognize, and they may obscure local variation within national borders. A country resized by national totals may contain enormous internal inequality that the map cannot show.

But these limitations do not weaken the project so much as define its purpose. The atlas is not trying to replace detailed local research, nor is it intended for navigation. Its strength is global comparison. It shows where phenomena are concentrated at the scale of nations and regions, and it does so in a way that is emotionally and intellectually immediate.

The maps work best as starting points. They provoke questions that lead to deeper inquiry: Why is the distribution of disease so uneven? How does trade reshape national economies? What explains the geography of migration? How do consumption and responsibility differ from population and need?

## Mapping the Way We Live

The title *The Atlas of the Real World* is deliberately provocative. It does not mean that conventional maps are unreal. Rather, it suggests that territory alone is not enough. The “real world” is also made of people, money, illness, energy, food, labor, technology, pollution, and movement. It is made of relationships and inequalities that cannot be seen from land area alone.

By redrawing the planet through equal-area cartograms, the atlas and its website give visual form to those hidden geographies. They show a world in which size is not fixed but depends on the question being asked. The same country can be vast in one reality and tiny in another. The same region can be central to one global story and marginal to the next.

That may be the project’s most enduring insight: maps do not merely show us where we are. They shape what we notice, what we value, and what we imagine to be possible. *The Atlas of the Real World* asks us to look again at a planet we thought we knew—and to recognize that the world’s true shape depends on the lives lived across it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed news piece about a project that redraws the world map according to statistics like disease, wealth, education, greenhouse emissions, dentists, and tractors.
counterfactuals.output:
**Project redraws the world by disease, wealth, education — even dentists and tractors**

A project that turns global statistics into striking, distorted world maps is offering a new way to understand inequality, development and environmental responsibility — by redrawing countries according to what they represent rather than how much land they occupy.

The project, widely known as **Worldmapper**, replaces the familiar geography of coastlines and borders with **cartograms**: maps in which each country is resized according to a particular statistic. Instead of showing Russia, Canada or Australia as vast simply because they cover enormous land areas, the maps swell or shrink nations according to measures such as population, income, disease burden, school enrolment, carbon emissions, number of doctors or dentists, and ownership of farm machinery such as tractors.

The result is a world that looks both recognizable and radically unfamiliar. On a map of global wealth, North America, Western Europe and Japan balloon outward while many poorer regions shrink dramatically. On maps of HIV/AIDS or malaria, parts of sub-Saharan Africa expand far beyond their conventional size. A map based on greenhouse gas emissions enlarges industrialized and fast-growing economies, revealing where climate-warming pollution has historically and currently been concentrated. Maps of education, health care access or agricultural equipment tell different stories again — about opportunity, infrastructure and uneven development.

The aim, according to the researchers and designers behind the project, is to make statistics visible in a way that tables and conventional maps often fail to do.

Traditional world maps are dominated by land area. That can mislead viewers, because land size is often unrelated to the human issues being discussed. A country with a vast territory but a small population may appear visually important on a standard map, while a densely populated or economically powerful country may appear comparatively modest. Cartograms reverse that emphasis: they ask viewers to see the world in proportion to people, money, illness, consumption or capacity.

In one map, countries are scaled according to **gross domestic product**, producing an image in which the United States, Europe and parts of East Asia dominate. In another, based on **child mortality** or infectious disease, the visual weight shifts toward countries facing the highest health burdens. A map of **dentists** highlights the unequal distribution of routine health services, with richer countries appearing swollen and many poorer nations nearly disappearing. A map of **tractors** offers an unusual but revealing proxy for agricultural mechanization, showing how access to technology varies across rural economies.

The project’s power lies partly in its simplicity. Each map uses the same basic principle: the area of a territory is made proportional to a selected statistic. If a country accounts for 10 percent of the world total for that measure, it is drawn to occupy roughly 10 percent of the map’s area. The shapes are distorted but kept near their geographic neighbors so that viewers can still identify regions and compare patterns.

The maps cover a wide range of themes, including:

- **Disease and health:** HIV/AIDS, malaria, tuberculosis, infant mortality, life expectancy, doctors, dentists and hospital beds.  
- **Wealth and poverty:** income, GDP, exports, imports, debt and consumption.  
- **Education:** literacy, primary and secondary enrolment, university participation and spending on education.  
- **Environment:** carbon dioxide emissions, energy use, fuel consumption and ecological impacts.  
- **Population and society:** births, migration, urban population, elderly population and children.  
- **Agriculture and technology:** tractors, cereal production, food imports and access to infrastructure.

For educators, journalists and policy researchers, the maps provide a vivid way to communicate global disparities. A lesson on climate change, for example, can use emissions cartograms to show the difference between where people live and where the most carbon pollution is produced. A discussion of public health can compare population maps with maps of disease prevalence or medical professionals, making clear that need and capacity are often badly mismatched.

The project also challenges assumptions embedded in the most familiar world map projections. Standard maps, especially those derived from the Mercator projection, exaggerate the size of countries farther from the equator and understate the visual prominence of many equatorial regions. Worldmapper does something different: it deliberately distorts geography not by projection accident, but by statistical meaning.

The images can be startling. The United States may loom on maps of wealth, military spending or emissions, but shrink on maps showing certain infectious diseases. India and China expand hugely on population-based maps, reflecting their demographic weight, while small but wealthy countries may become prominent on measures of finance, trade or technology. Africa’s outline changes dramatically depending on whether the subject is land area, population, disease, mineral extraction or agricultural capacity.

Critics of cartograms note that they can oversimplify complex issues. A country enlarged on a disease map may contain enormous internal variation; national averages can hide regional inequalities, ethnic disparities or urban-rural divides. Wealth maps based on total GDP may favor large economies, while per-person measures tell a different story. Data quality also varies, especially in countries with weaker statistical systems or in measures that rely on estimates.

The project’s creators acknowledge those limitations but argue that the maps are not meant to replace detailed analysis. Rather, they serve as entry points — visual provocations that invite questions. Why does this region expand on one map and contract on another? Why do places with high disease burdens often have fewer medical professionals? Why do emissions maps look so different from population maps? Why does agricultural machinery cluster in some regions and not others?

By presenting hundreds of global datasets in the same visual format, the project allows patterns to emerge across subjects. It shows that the world’s inequalities are not confined to one category. Wealth, education, health care, energy use and technological capacity tend to overlap, but not perfectly. Some countries perform strongly in education despite modest income; others have high emissions without comparable population size; still others bear disproportionate health burdens while contributing little to global wealth or pollution.

The inclusion of unusual indicators — such as dentists and tractors — is part of the project’s appeal. Dentists may sound like a narrow measure, but they point toward broader questions of health infrastructure, income, training and access to routine care. Tractors reveal something about agricultural productivity, capital investment and the mechanization gap between farming systems. These unconventional maps remind viewers that development is not a single number but a web of resources, services and opportunities.

At a time when global debates often revolve around inequality, pandemic preparedness, climate responsibility and access to education, the project offers a visual language for comparing the scale of problems and resources. It transforms abstract numbers into shapes that are difficult to ignore.

The familiar classroom world map suggests a planet divided mainly by territory. Worldmapper’s distorted atlas suggests something else: a planet divided by chances — the chance to survive childhood, to attend school, to receive medical care, to consume energy, to emit carbon, to own machinery, to accumulate wealth.

In these maps, geography is not abandoned. It is reimagined. The world is redrawn not as it looks from space, but as it is experienced through statistics.
